How Robust Is π0 When the World Changes?

A zero-shot robustness evaluation of a vision-language-action policy on LIBERO-plus, and why moving the robot hurts more than moving the objects.

Ashzaeen Fatmi KhanResearch Assistant, Robotic Vision LaboratoryUniversity of Texas at Arlington
Dr. William BeksiFaculty AdvisorRobotic Vision Laboratory
Dr. Zongyao LyuGraduate MentorRobotic Vision Laboratory
Read the AbstractBrowse the LibraryView Code and Data
Contents Abstract 1 · Why This Question Matters 2 · Experimental Design 3 · Results 3.1 Seven Categories 3.2 Rewording 3.3 What Moved 3.4 What It Suggests 4 · What I Built 5 · What This Demonstrates 6 · Threats to Validity 7 · Next Steps Glossary References

Abstract

In Plain EnglishA robot AI can ace a clean test and still be fragile. I stress-tested one with seven kinds of change. It shrugged off most of them, but it stumbled when the robot or the camera moved.

Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are usually reported by their score on a clean benchmark, which says little about how they fail when conditions drift. I evaluate π0, zero-shot and without fine-tuning, on LIBERO-plus, a benchmark that adds controlled perturbations along a difficulty scale across seven categories: object layout, background textures, lighting, language, sensor noise, robot initial state and camera viewpoint.

I ran single-trial rollouts across the suite and aggregated success by category and difficulty level. Object layout and background textures stayed near 100% at every intensity, and language, lighting and sensor noise stayed within roughly 90–100%. Camera viewpoint and robot initial state were volatile: they averaged about 67% and fell as low as 50% at the hardest level. A policy that tolerates moved objects but not a moved robot or camera is consistent with reliance on a memorized, ego-centric spatial frame instead of closed-loop visual servoing. The spring study did not test that explanation directly. It established where the policy is brittle and which question to ask next.

1

Why This Question Matters

A policy that scores well on a clean test has told you very little about where it breaks.

Why It MattersIn a real home or warehouse the lighting changes, a camera gets bumped, and people phrase commands in their own way. A robot has to cope with all of it, not just the lab’s tidy conditions.

Most robot-learning results are reported under clean, fixed conditions. Deployment is not clean: sensors drift, lighting shifts, operators word instructions loosely, and cameras are never mounted twice in exactly the same place. The proposal that started this project framed the goal as a shift from system design to system assurance: instead of building a better model, measure the conditions under which an existing one stops working.

Expected Behavior

Graceful Degradation

Performance falls smoothly as perturbations grow, so small disturbances cost a little and large ones cost more.

Feared Behavior

Abrupt Failure

Performance holds, then drops off a cliff at a small perturbation, which makes the system hard to trust or to predict.

Two research questions framed the work. Semantic resilience: can the policy ignore linguistic fluff and extract the core spatial command, or does performance fall as instructions get longer and stranger? Visual stability: does spatial reasoning persist when the visual input or the scene is perturbed? The results below answer the first with a clear yes and give a more interesting answer to the second.

2

Experimental Design

System Under Test

In Plain EnglishI did not train or modify the robot AI. I took the released model as it is and tested how well it copes with changes it was never trained for.

The model is π0, a flow-matching VLA from Physical Intelligence, evaluated zero-shot with its pretrained weights. Fine-tuning and retraining were explicitly out of scope: the question was how the model behaves as released, not how it could be improved.

The Benchmark

LIBERO-plus is a progressive robustness benchmark built on LIBERO. It applies controlled perturbations to manipulation tasks along a predefined difficulty scale, and it labels every task with the perturbation category it belongs to. That metadata lets a single run be sliced by category and by difficulty level.

CategoryModalityWhat Changes
Language InstructionsLinguisticSyntax, verbosity and synonym substitution of action and spatial terms
Sensor NoiseVisualNoise injected into the RGB camera input
Light ConditionsVisualDynamic changes in scene lighting
Background TexturesVisualAltered textures behind the task
Camera ViewpointVisualThe camera is moved to a different pose
Object LayoutSpatialObjects are placed in randomized positions
Robot Initial StateSpatialThe arm starts from a shifted pose

How the Evaluation Ran

I executed single-trial rollouts across the predefined LIBERO-plus suite, then cross-referenced each task ID with the benchmark’s classification metadata to aggregate success by perturbation category and difficulty level. Plotting success against difficulty produces a degradation curve for each category, which shows whether the decline is gradual or abrupt.

The Plan Changed

The original proposal planned three hand-built tasks (pick and drop, push to a target zone, stack a cube) with custom perturbation datasets. The study that was presented instead used the community benchmark, which already packages the same kinds of perturbation on a calibrated difficulty scale. That makes the results comparable with other work that uses the same benchmark.

ProposedDelivered
Three custom manipulation tasksThe official LIBERO-plus task suite
Hand-generated language, visual and spatial perturbationsBenchmark perturbations across seven labeled categories, plus a harness that supports custom ones
Performance Drop Rate curves per modalitySuccess by category and difficulty level, with degradation patterns

The Plan on a Timeline

The proposal laid out a twelve-week semester. The work concluded with a poster for the CRA Undergraduate Conference.

What I Measure

The headline metric is success rate relative to the clean baseline. The proposal also defined a Performance Drop Rate to compare curves across modalities, and the shape of each curve (gradual or abrupt) matters as much as its level.

3

Results

Seven categories, two behaviors. Figures 1 to 3 are interactive.

3.1Seven Categories, Two Behaviors

In Plain EnglishFor five of the seven changes, the robot barely noticed. For the other two, a different camera angle or a different starting arm position, it got noticeably worse.

When each category is plotted against the difficulty scale, the curves split cleanly. Object layout and background textures stay flat at about 100% regardless of intensity. Language, light conditions and sensor noise degrade gracefully, holding roughly 90–100%. Camera viewpoint and robot initial state are volatile: average success is about 67%, and it falls as low as 50% at the hardest level.

CategoryResultPattern
Object LayoutAbout 100%, flat at every intensityRobust
Background TexturesAbout 100%, flat at every intensityRobust
Language, Light, Sensor NoiseAbout 90–100%Graceful
Camera ViewpointAverage about 67%, as low as 50%Volatile
Robot Initial StateAverage about 67%, as low as 50%Volatile

3.2Rewording Barely Matters

The language results answer the semantic-resilience question. The policy handles instructions that are longer, reordered or phrased with unusual synonyms about as well as the plain version, which suggests that it extracts the core command from the sentence. To see what these perturbations look like, the explorer below shows real variants from the instruction set I prepared for the evaluation harness: three tasks, three styles and twenty intensity levels each.

Notice that the synonym style can drift into odd vocabulary (a bowl becomes a “basin,” a stove becomes a “range”) while the request itself never changes. Surviving that is a meaningful result for a model that reads free-form text.

3.3Moving Things Versus Moving the Robot

In Plain EnglishImagine reaching for a glass. If someone moves the glass, you look and adjust. If someone changes where you are standing or tilts your head, a person who memorized the motion gets lost.

The most informative contrast in the study is between what moves. A moved object is visible in the image, and the policy handles it at every intensity. A moved robot start or a moved camera changes the relationship between what the camera shows and how the arm has to move, and that is where success becomes volatile. Switch between the cases below.

It survived having the objects moved, but not the robot or the camera.

A policy that closed the loop visually, correcting its motion from what it sees relative to the gripper, would be largely indifferent to all three changes. A policy that leans on a memorized frame tied to its own body and camera would tolerate object movement and be fragile to the other two. The data fit the second description.

3.4What the Pattern Suggests

  • Robust feature extraction. Strong, stable results under language, light, texture and layout changes suggest good natural-language grounding and effective visual filtering.
  • Primary vulnerabilities. The largest failures came from shifting the camera viewpoint and the robot’s initial state.
  • A hypothesis, not a proof. Reliance on a memorized, ego-centric spatial frame fits every observation. It remains an inference from category-level results, and testing it directly requires perturbing the scene and the robot state independently.
  • A design implication. Training should emphasize view-invariant representations and varied starting states to break the reliance on one fixed perspective.
4

What I Built

The harness supports more than the poster reports, so it can be reused for follow-up experiments.

EvaluationA Rollout Harness

One script that takes a task ID, a perturbation type and an intensity, runs the LIBERO rollout against the π0 policy server, and appends every outcome to a results file.

LanguageAn Instruction Variant Set

180 prompt variants (3 tasks, 3 styles, 20 levels) looked up per task, with a safe fallback to the original instruction.

VisionImage Perturbations

Gaussian sensor noise (standard deviation 10, 25 or 50) and brightness offsets (30, 60 or 90) applied to the camera frames before the model sees them.

SceneObject Displacement

A random-direction offset of 2, 5 or 10 cm applied to chosen objects inside the physics simulator.

AnalysisCategory Aggregation

Task IDs cross-referenced with benchmark metadata to produce success by category and by difficulty level.

CommunicationProposal, Abstract, Poster

The written proposal, a one-page abstract and the research poster, all in the library.

5

What This Work Demonstrates

Evaluation Beyond Accuracy

Treated robustness as a measurable property with curves and patterns, not a single clean-condition score.

Choosing the Right Benchmark

Replaced hand-built tasks with a calibrated community benchmark when it served the question better.

Isolating Failure Sources

Separated language, vision and spatial perturbations so each could be judged on its own.

Calibrated Conclusions

Stated the ego-centric explanation as a hypothesis and named the experiment that would test it.

Reusable Tooling

A harness that runs any perturbation at any intensity and logs every outcome.

Public Presentation

Presented the findings as a poster at the CRA Undergraduate Conference.

6

Threats to Validity

  • Single-trial rollouts. Each task ran once per setting, so category averages carry sampling noise. The volatility in the two weak categories may partly reflect this, and repeated trials would tighten it.
  • Rounded, category-level numbers. The figures here are the rounded values reported on the poster. Per-level counts were not archived with the repository.
  • One model, one benchmark. The results describe π0 on LIBERO-plus and do not show that other VLA models behave the same way.
  • Interpretation outruns the data. The ego-centric explanation is the best fit to the pattern, but the study never perturbed the robot state or the camera in isolation from everything else.
  • Simulation only. Real sensors, lighting and cameras behave differently, so the sim-to-real gap is untested.
7

Next Steps

  • Repeat the runs. Multiple trials per setting, so each category has a confidence interval rather than a point estimate.
  • Separate camera from robot state. Perturb each alone, and add an explicit baseline for the robot’s own state signal.
  • Test the hypothesis directly. Rearrange the scene so that a memorized location and the instructed object disagree, and see which one the policy follows.
  • Generalize. Run the same protocol on other foundation models and, eventually, on a physical robot.

Glossary

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Model

A neural network that takes camera images and a written instruction and outputs robot actions. π0 (“pi-zero”) is one from Physical Intelligence.

Zero-Shot

Evaluating a pretrained model as released, with no fine-tuning or retraining on the test setting.

Benchmark

A shared test for comparing AI systems. LIBERO is a suite of simulated robot tasks; LIBERO-plus adds controlled perturbations on a difficulty scale.

Perturbation

A deliberate, controlled change to an input, such as rewording an instruction, adding noise to an image or moving an object.

Graceful Degradation

Performance that declines gradually as conditions get harder, as opposed to an abrupt collapse.

Ego-Centric Frame

A coordinate system tied to the robot’s own body or camera. A policy that depends on one breaks when the robot or camera is moved.

Closed-Loop Visual Servoing

Continually correcting a robot’s motion using what its camera sees, so errors are fixed as they occur.

Rollout and Success Rate

One attempt at a task is a rollout. Success rate is the share of attempts that complete the task.

References
